bpa.subtitle: A BOTIA Women's Health Alert · Understanding Food Labels
bpa.aliases-value: Tin can linings, plastic bottles, food container coatings, thermal receipt paper
bpa.description: BPA is a chemical used in the production of polycarbonate plastics and epoxy resins. It is found in the inner lining of many food and drink cans, and in some plastic containers. It does not appear on ingredient lists — but it migrates into food.
bpa.uses-value: Canned tomatoes, canned fish, canned beans, plastic bottles, food storage containers
bpa.section-what-means: What It Means for Women's Health
bpa.plain-explanation: BPA is an endocrine disruptor — it mimics oestrogen in the body. Women are particularly vulnerable because of hormonal sensitivity. BPA accumulates in fatty tissue and has been linked to hormonal disruption, reproductive effects, and thyroid interference.
bpa.everyday-value: That canned tomato sauce you use every week? The lining of the can may be releasing BPA into your food, especially when the contents are acidic or heated.
bpa.why-explanation: BOTIA detected packaging or processing conditions associated with BPA exposure in this product. BPA is not listed as an ingredient — but its presence in packaging is documented by EFSA and WHO.
bpa.display-logic: BPA-associated packaging detected → Women's Health Alert
bpa.can-1: Products in cans with epoxy resin linings
bpa.can-3: Acidic products in cans (tomatoes, citrus, vinegar-based)
bpa.cannot-1: Tell you what to consume or avoid — that is your decision
bpa.cannot-2: Measure actual BPA levels in this specific product
bpa.cannot-3: Confirm whether this manufacturer uses BPA-free linings
bpa.cannot-note: BOTIA provides documented context from EFSA and WHO reports. Personal health decisions are yours. If you have concerns about endocrine disruptors, consult a healthcare professional.
bpa.sources-items: EFSA BPA re-evaluation 2023 · WHO endocrine disruptors report · European Food Safety Authority · ANSES (French Agency for Food Safety)

parabens_e214.subtitle: A BOTIA Women's Health Alert · Understanding Food Labels
parabens_e214.aliases-value: Methylparaben, Ethylparaben, Propylparaben, Butylparaben, Sodium methylparaben
parabens_e214.description: Parabens are preservatives used in food, cosmetics, and pharmaceuticals. In food, they appear as E numbers E214–E219. They have weak oestrogenic activity — meaning they can interact with hormone receptors in the body.
parabens_e214.uses-value: Processed foods, bakery products, some beverages, jams, sauces, some medications
parabens_e214.section-what-means: What It Means for Women's Health
parabens_e214.plain-explanation: Parabens mimic oestrogen at a low level. Their concern for women comes from cumulative exposure — from food, cosmetics, and personal care products simultaneously. Research has detected parabens in breast tissue. Their long-term hormonal effects are under active scientific review.
parabens_e214.everyday-value: You may be absorbing parabens from your food AND your skincare at the same time. The cumulative load is what researchers are concerned about.
parabens_e214.why-explanation: BOTIA detected parabens (E214–E219) on this product's label. These preservatives have documented oestrogenic activity and are flagged by EFSA for ongoing monitoring.
parabens_e214.display-logic: Parabens with oestrogenic activity detected → Women's Health Alert
parabens_e214.can-1: E214 (ethyl p-hydroxybenzoate) and its sodium salt E215
parabens_e214.can-2: E216 (propyl p-hydroxybenzoate) and its sodium salt E217
parabens_e214.can-3: E218 (methyl p-hydroxybenzoate) and its sodium salt E219
parabens_e214.can-4: Methylparaben, ethylparaben, propylparaben listed by name
parabens_e214.cannot-1: Tell you what to consume or avoid — that is your decision
parabens_e214.cannot-2: Quantify your total daily paraben exposure
parabens_e214.cannot-3: Assess interaction with cosmetic paraben exposure
parabens_e214.cannot-note: EFSA has restricted use of propyl and butyl parabens in foods for infants. Research on adult cumulative exposure is ongoing.
parabens_e214.sources-items: EFSA parabens opinion · WHO endocrine disruptors · Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety (SCCS) · Environmental Health Perspectives

e171.subtitle: A BOTIA Women's Health Alert · Understanding Food Labels
e171.description: E171 is a white pigment used to whiten and brighten food products. It consists of titanium dioxide particles, some of which are in the nanoscale range. EFSA concluded in 2021 that E171 can no longer be considered safe as a food additive, citing genotoxicity concerns.
e171.uses-value: Chewing gum, sugar coatings on sweets and medications, white sauces, some cheeses, bakery products
e171.section-what-means: What It Means for Women's Health
e171.plain-explanation: Nanoparticles of titanium dioxide can cross biological barriers. EFSA's 2021 opinion flagged genotoxicity — meaning potential DNA damage. Women of reproductive age and during pregnancy are considered a priority concern group in ongoing research.
e171.everyday-value: That white coating on your chewing gum or the white filling in some sweets may contain titanium dioxide nanoparticles. The EU banned E171 in food from 2022, but it may still appear in products from outside the EU.
e171.why-explanation: BOTIA detected E171 on this label. The EU banned E171 in food in 2022 following EFSA's safety opinion. Its presence in non-EU products or legacy stock warrants flagging.
e171.display-logic: E171 detected — banned in EU food since 2022 → Women's Health Alert
e171.cannot-1: Tell you what to consume or avoid — that is your decision
e171.cannot-2: Determine the particle size of E171 in this specific product
e171.cannot-3: Confirm whether this is EU-produced or imported stock
e171.cannot-note: E171 is banned as a food additive in the EU since August 2022. It may still appear in products imported from outside the EU or in legacy stock.
e171.sources-items: EFSA E171 safety opinion 2021 · EU Commission Regulation 2022/63 · WHO nanoparticles safety review · ANSES

alert_endocrine.subtitle: A BOTIA Women's Health Context · Understanding Food Labels
alert_endocrine.aliases-value: Multiple additives with potential hormonal activity detected in this product
alert_endocrine.description: This product contains one or more additives that have been identified in scientific literature as having potential endocrine-disrupting activity. These are substances that can interfere with the hormonal system — not through a single dramatic effect, but through cumulative, low-level exposure over time.
alert_endocrine.uses-value: The endocrine system regulates metabolism, reproduction, sleep, mood, and growth. Disruption — even at low doses — can have long-term effects that are difficult to trace back to a specific exposure.
alert_endocrine.section-what-means: What It Means for Women's Health
alert_endocrine.plain-explanation: Women's hormonal systems are more complex and more sensitive to external interference than men's. The menstrual cycle, fertility, pregnancy, menopause — all involve delicate hormonal balance. Endocrine disruptors accumulate in fatty tissue (women typically have more) and their effects compound over years of daily exposure.
alert_endocrine.everyday-value: No single product is the problem. The problem is daily exposure to dozens of low-level disruptors across food, packaging, and personal care. BOTIA makes that exposure visible.
alert_endocrine.why-explanation: BOTIA detected additives in this product that are flagged in EFSA or WHO reports for potential endocrine activity. This is a contextual alert — not a prohibition. It is information that the food system does not normally surface for you.
alert_endocrine.display-logic: Additives with potential hormonal activity detected → Women's Health Context Alert
alert_endocrine.can-1: Additives flagged in EFSA endocrine disruptor assessments
alert_endocrine.can-3: Colorants and emulsifiers under hormonal review
alert_endocrine.can-4: Packaging migrants known to interfere with hormone receptors
alert_endocrine.cannot-1: Tell you what to consume or avoid — that is your decision
alert_endocrine.cannot-2: Quantify your total daily endocrine disruptor load
alert_endocrine.cannot-note: This alert reflects documented scientific concern, not established harm from this product alone. The concern is cumulative and long-term.
alert_endocrine.sources-items: EFSA endocrine disruptor framework · WHO/UNEP State of the Science of Endocrine Disrupting Chemicals · European Environment Agency · ANSES

alert_fat_accumulation.subtitle: A BOTIA Women's Health Context · Understanding Food Labels
alert_fat_accumulation.aliases-value: Fat-soluble additives accumulate in adipose tissue and release during periods of rapid fat loss
alert_fat_accumulation.description: Some food additives, pesticide residues, and packaging migrants are lipophilic — they dissolve in fat, not water. This means they accumulate in fatty tissue over years of exposure. When the body burns fat rapidly (during dieting, illness, breastfeeding, or menopause), these stored compounds release into the bloodstream in concentrated form.
alert_fat_accumulation.uses-value: Rapid weight loss diets, intermittent fasting, illness-related weight loss, breastfeeding (toxins pass to milk), perimenopause (hormonal fat redistribution)
alert_fat_accumulation.section-what-means: What It Means for Women's Health
alert_fat_accumulation.plain-explanation: Women typically have a higher percentage of body fat than men, which means more storage capacity for fat-soluble compounds. When women lose weight quickly — especially through restrictive diets — years of accumulated fat-soluble toxins can release suddenly into the bloodstream. This can cause symptoms including fatigue, brain fog, hormonal disruption, and feeling unwell during what should be a healthy process.
alert_fat_accumulation.everyday-value: If you start a strict diet and feel terrible despite doing everything right — it may not be lack of willpower. It may be stored toxins releasing from fat tissue. This is real, documented, and almost never discussed.
alert_fat_accumulation.why-explanation: This product contains fat-soluble additives that may contribute to long-term adipose tissue accumulation. BOTIA surfaces this context because it is almost never communicated in food labelling or public health messaging.
alert_fat_accumulation.display-logic: Fat-soluble additives detected → Fat accumulation context alert for women
alert_fat_accumulation.can-1: Fat-soluble colorants (azo dyes, fat-soluble E numbers)
alert_fat_accumulation.can-4: Products with high fat content combined with multiple additives
alert_fat_accumulation.cannot-1: Tell you what to consume or avoid — that is your decision
alert_fat_accumulation.cannot-2: Measure your personal toxin accumulation level
alert_fat_accumulation.cannot-note: The phenomenon of toxin release during fat mobilisation is documented in clinical literature. If you are experiencing unexpected symptoms during weight loss, speak with a healthcare professional.
alert_fat_accumulation.sources-items: WHO persistent organic pollutants review · EFSA lipophilic contaminants · Journal of Exposure Science & Environmental Epidemiology · Environmental Health Perspectives

alert_packaging.subtitle: A BOTIA Women's Health Context · Understanding Food Labels
alert_packaging.aliases-value: Chemical compounds from packaging materials that transfer into food during storage, transport, or heating
alert_packaging.description: Food packaging is not inert. Plastics, can linings, paper coatings, and plastic films release chemical compounds into food — especially when food is acidic, fatty, or hot. These compounds do not appear on ingredient lists. They include BPA, phthalates, PFAS, mineral oils, and adhesive residues.
alert_packaging.uses-value: Heating food in plastic containers, canned acidic foods (tomatoes, citrus), fatty foods in plastic packaging, long storage in plastic wrap, microwave packaging
alert_packaging.section-what-means: What It Means for Women's Health
alert_packaging.plain-explanation: Many packaging migrants are endocrine disruptors. They enter the body through food and accumulate over time. Women's hormonal systems are more sensitive to external hormonal interference. The effects are cumulative — no single exposure causes harm, but years of daily exposure adds up.
alert_packaging.everyday-value: Never microwave food in plastic containers. Never store acidic food in plastic. These are not paranoia — they are based on documented chemical migration data.
alert_packaging.why-explanation: This product is packaged in materials associated with chemical migration risk. The packaging itself is not listed as an ingredient, but its interaction with the food content is documented.
alert_packaging.display-logic: High-migration packaging type detected → Packaging migrant context alert
alert_packaging.can-1: Canned products with acidic content (migration risk)
alert_packaging.can-2: Fatty products in flexible plastic packaging
alert_packaging.can-3: Products intended to be heated in their packaging
alert_packaging.can-4: Products with long shelf life in plastic containers
alert_packaging.cannot-1: Tell you what to consume or avoid — that is your decision
alert_packaging.cannot-2: Measure actual migrant levels in this specific product
alert_packaging.cannot-3: Confirm which specific migrants are present
alert_packaging.cannot-note: EU Regulation 10/2011 governs plastic food contact materials. Compliance with regulations does not mean zero migration — it means migration below established thresholds, which are under ongoing scientific review.
alert_packaging.sources-items: EU Regulation 10/2011 on plastic food contact materials · EFSA food contact materials panel · WHO BPA assessment · ANSES packaging migrants report
